name: Ivan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Ivan. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new connections crew for the power company. When a builder puts up a new housing estate, or someone builds a solar farm out on the edge of town, we're the ones who run the lines in and hook it up to the grid. It's mostly fresh work, new poles, new cable, nothing rotten or patched, which I like. Right now we're connecting a two-hundred-house estate off the bypass, and I'm there most of this month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a little company on the side, two years old now. Weekends, I fly a drone over roofs and give people quotes for solar panels, and I do some inspection flights for farmers. I use AI every day for it, the quotes, the invoices, planning flights. I live with my girlfriend Hana, she's a dental hygienist, and I own a studio flat I rent out, so I've got a decent cushion. My grandfather ran a bakery for forty years, so I guess running something is in the blood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always a tool, not a miracle, and good tools are worth having. I'd probably post something on the business page about how I use it, because it's a selling point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plans carry on. Build the business slowly, keep the day job for the steady money and the pension. Nothing in this picture breaks anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep the weekends going, maybe buy a second drone and hire my cousin for the busy months. Keep the studio rented.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually. Steady growth suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does AI actually do for your side business now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of the boring part. I fly the roof, it helps me work out panel layout and payback, and it writes the quote in a minute. That used to take me a whole evening. It saves me probably eight hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever go full-time on the business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a few years, if it keeps growing. But I'm not reckless. A steady wage from the power company is a good foundation, and I'd only jump when the numbers say jump.

S0.say: He'd say AI was always a tool rather than a miracle and good tools are worth having. He'd post about how he uses it on his business page as a selling point.
S0.think: He thinks his plans carry on: grow the side business slowly and keep the day job for steady pay and the pension. Nothing in this picture breaks anything.
S0.do: Keeps his weekend drone and solar quoting business going, possibly buys a second drone and hires his cousin for busy months. Keeps renting out his studio flat.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, because steady growth suits him.
S0.quote: That used to take me a whole evening. It saves me probably eight hours a week.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is an entrepreneur on the side and already gets real time savings from AI. His caution about leaving a steady wage shows a careful streak beneath his comfort with risk. He links his drive to run something to his grandfather's bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for anyone willing to learn. The people who moan will get left behind, and the people who adapt will do fine. I'd say that at work too, though maybe more politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well out of this. The day job stays mostly the same, and my side business gets more efficient. I'd be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring more AI into the business, automatic flight plans, a booking system, maybe a second drone that maps roofs on its own. I'd put some savings into new kit. In the day job I'd be first to try any new tool the company offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk to the day job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. New connections still need people setting poles and pulling cable. Maybe fewer planners and designers back at the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You value hard work and apprenticeships. How does that fit with automating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't see a clash. Hard work means doing the job well with the best tools you can get. My grandfather bought a bigger oven when he could afford one, nobody called that lazy.

S1.say: He'd say it's an opportunity for anyone willing to learn, and those who complain will be left behind. He'd say it more politely at work.
S1.think: He thinks he'd do well: the day job stays mostly the same and his side business becomes more efficient. He'd be quietly pleased.
S1.do: Brings more AI into his business, including automatic flight plans, a booking system and possibly a self-mapping second drone, and puts savings into new equipment. Is first to try any new tool at the day job.
S1.quote: My grandfather bought a bigger oven when he could afford one, nobody called that lazy.
S1.fieldNote: He sees no conflict between valuing hard work and automating, and used his grandfather's bakery to explain why. He expects office planning jobs to shrink before field work. His tone toward people who resist change is a bit sharp in private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd mean it. But I'd also say the government shouldn't hand the big companies all the advantages, because small businesses need a fair shot. Owning the machines can't just be for the giants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my day job is gone in this picture, and probably fast, because new-build work is the easiest for robots: clean sites, simple designs. So the business is my future, if I can make it work in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand in my notice at the power company within six months and go full-time on the business. I'd buy whatever robots and drones came on the market first, even on credit, and offer connection and solar work to builders. I'd sell the studio flat if I needed the cash to buy kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but buzzing too. Like the night before a big job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be buying robots that do what you do now. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone's going to own them. I'd rather it was me than a giant company in another city. It's no different from my grandfather and his oven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is fast. What's the risk for a small business like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big firms buy all the robots first and undercut everyone. Two years isn't long to build a name. That's the bit that keeps me up, not the robots themselves.

S2.say: He'd say adapt or get left behind, while arguing government shouldn't give big companies every advantage because owning the machines can't be only for giants. Small businesses need a fair shot.
S2.think: He thinks his day job would go fast because new-build sites are the easiest for robots, so his business would be his future, if he can make it work in two years.
S2.do: Resigns from the power company within six months to run his business full-time, buys the first robots and drones available, even on credit, and offers connection and solar work to builders. Sells the studio flat if he needs cash for equipment.
S2.feel: Uneasy but buzzing, like the night before a big job.
S2.quote: I'd rather it was me than a giant company in another city.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan moves toward risk fast here, and his plan is bold: quit, borrow, sell the flat. His worry isn't the robots but big firms buying them first and undercutting small ones. He identified new-build work as especially easy to automate, which sharpened his urgency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message: learn, adapt, own something. I'd tell the apprentices on the crew to learn robotics alongside their lines training. That's the apprenticeship of the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is perfect for me. Long enough to build the business properly, short enough that the people who wait will be too late. I'd be thirty-two with a real company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job for two or three more years while growing the business, then leave once it pays me properly. I'd buy robots as soon as they're reliable, not the first shaky ones. I'd keep the studio flat as a safety net and put most of my savings into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Focused. Like having a clear plan for the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change the plan compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'd gamble. Five years means I can do it properly, test the robots, pick the right ones, keep the flat. It's less exciting but smarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Hana? Would this change your plans together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about getting married in a couple of years. I don't think this changes that. If anything, I'd want something solid built before kids, and five years lets me do that.

S3.say: He'd repeat learn, adapt and own something, and urge apprentices to learn robotics alongside their lines training as the apprenticeship of the future.
S3.think: He thinks five years is perfect for him: long enough to build the business properly but short enough that those who wait will be too late. He'd be thirty-two with a real company.
S3.do: Keeps the day job for two or three more years while growing the business, then leaves once it pays properly. Buys robots once reliable, keeps the studio flat as a safety net and puts most of his savings into the business.
S3.feel: Calm and focused, like having a clear plan for the week.
S3.quote: Two years means I'd gamble. Five years means I can do it properly, test the robots, pick the right ones, keep the flat.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is his ideal timeline and turns a gamble into a measured plan. His traditional values show in wanting something solid built before children, and in framing robotics as the new apprenticeship. Marriage plans with Hana stay on course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's plenty of time, so nobody has an excuse. Learn a skill, save, start something. That's what I'd tell anyone at work or online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is fine, maybe a bit slow. More competitors would see it coming too. But I'd have a decade to grow the business and get married and have kids before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job longer, maybe five or six years, and grow the business steadily. I'd keep buying new kit as it proved itself. Hana and I would get married as planned, and I'd keep the studio rented.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too slow for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. When everyone has ten years, everyone gets ready. The advantage of moving first is smaller. But it's also less risky, so I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep taxes low for small firms, back apprenticeships for the new kind of work, and don't give the big companies special deals. Let people compete. That's all I'd ask.

S4.say: He'd say a decade leaves nobody an excuse: learn a skill, save and start something. He'd tell that to anyone at work or online.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is fine, if a little slow, because competitors would see it coming too. He'd have a decade to grow the business, marry and have children before it arrives.
S4.do: Keeps the day job for five or six more years while growing the business and buys new equipment as it proves itself. Marries as planned and keeps the studio flat rented.
S4.quote: When everyone has ten years, everyone gets ready.
S4.fieldNote: Unusually, Ivan sees a longer warning as a slight disadvantage, because his edge from moving first shrinks. His policy wishes are consistent with his free-market views: low taxes for small firms, apprenticeships and no special deals for large companies. Family plans stay on track throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but not because of the robots. It's that two years isn't enough time for a small business to get going before the big firms buy everything up. What would help is a fair shot: low taxes for small firms, no special deals for giants, and apprenticeships in looking after robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the machines in your town. If it's local people, the money stays local. If it's a company three hundred kilometres away, the town's just a place they plug in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: If it's a company three hundred kilometres away, the town's just a place they plug in.
portrait: Ivan Nakamura is a 27-year-old lineworker on a new connections crew, hooking up housing estates and solar farms to the grid. He lives with his girlfriend Hana, owns a rented studio flat and runs a weekend drone and solar quoting business, using AI every day for quotes and flight plans. He is calm and optimistic about milder change, which he sees as better tools. A two-year AGI warning makes him uneasy but excited; he would quit his job, buy robots on credit and race the big firms. With five or ten years he plans a measured move into his own company, and his main worry throughout is large companies, not robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years isn't enough for a small business to get going before big firms buy up the robots.
whatWouldHelp: A fair shot for small businesses: low taxes, no special deals for big firms and apprenticeships in looking after robots.
